metadata.purpose: Cleaned, codebase-ready transcripts for AI ingestion
notes: These were cleaned from user-provided speech-to-text transcripts.
Timestamps, filler, and obvious transcription noise were removed.
Proper names, book titles, and some place names were standardized where public sources supported the spelling.
Historical claims in the transcript bodies are the speaker's claims unless separately verified.
Unresolved details are marked as [unclear] rather than guessed.

Oríkì: odii (when clearly referring to praise poems)
òrun: odun (when clearly referring to heaven/invisible realm)

transcripts.title: Timotea 'Latuán' Albear
transcripts.topic: Historical figure associated with Havana Ocha
transcripts.cleaned_transcript:
Santo El back with another video. As promised, let's look at the historical figure **Latuán**. I have my notes, and yes, this is going to be a long one. This is actually my second time recording it because I stumbled over my words, and I want to be as accurate as possible.

My sources for this are a documentary the speaker refers to in the original transcript, plus **Obá Miguel “Willie” Ramos's** book **Orí Eledá Mí Ó… If My Head Does Not Sell Me**. I want to cite my sources so nobody thinks I'm just talking out of my ass.

The woman most people call **Latuán** was born circa **1844** and died in either **1935 or 1936**; the speaker leans toward **1935**. She is presented here as one of the major founders of **Havana Ocha**, and one of the key architects of the standardized **Havana style of initiation** as people know it today. The speaker frames her as working side by side with **Efunché**, and as one of the main forces behind the Havana form of the religion.

No verified photographs of Latuán are known to the speaker in this transcript. In the documentary he cites, an elder described her as a very pretty, voluptuous woman and used the word *mulata*, so the speaker tries to give the audience some visual sense of her even though the historical visual record is thin.

In this account, **Latuán was Efunché's right hand** and served as a major **oriaté** in Havana. The speaker places her period of major activity roughly between **1873 and 1915**, maybe extending a little later, while noting that if she died in 1935 she would have been elderly and probably not doing the same level of ritual work in her last years. He says that while Efunché was alive, Latuán functioned as her exclusive or principal ritual counterpart, and that after **Efunché's death in 1903**, Havana essentially became “Latuán's city.”

The speaker says Latuán arrived in Cuba in **1863**, and that she is generally believed to have come from **Oyo, Nigeria**, or at least from Yoruba land strongly associated with Oyo. His reasoning is that **Havana Ocha** is deeply **Oyo-centric** and heavily **Changó-centric**, especially in the way santo is seated on the head in Havana. Based on that ritual orientation, he believes Latuán most likely came from Oyo.

According to the account he cites, Latuán was an **emancipated would-be slave**. In other words, she was taken from Nigeria and brought toward Cuba with the intention of being enslaved, but her ship was captured by the British in **1863**. The speaker gives historical context: Britain had already abolished slavery, Haiti had abolished it in **1804**, Cuba did not officially stop participating in the slave trade until **1867**, and slavery in Cuba was not fully abolished until **1886**. By that time, he says, both **Havana Ocha** and **Matanzas Ocha** were already well underway.

The British intercepted the ship near Cuba. In the speaker's telling, the captives were then turned over to wealthy Cuban households so they could be educated. That matters because he presents Latuán as someone who was intended for slavery but who did **not** live out the same plantation life many others endured. He does, however, stress that the Middle Passage itself would still have been hell.

He says Latuán was regarded as especially educated and cultured because she wound up living among the social elites of Cuba. According to the documentary, she may have been initiated to **Changó** around the age of **thirteen** in Africa. The speaker also raises the possibility that **Efunché** may later have crowned her in Cuba and treated her as a daughter.

He later notes that **Willie Ramos** gives not just the year **1863**, but the date **July 12, 1863** for Latuán's arrival. He also mentions a historical document tied to that arrival that, according to the story he is repeating, was at one point borrowed for study and not promptly returned to the family. He says Ramos's book contains details and images related to that document.

The transcript then moves to Latuán's death. The speaker says she died on **February 5, 1935**, and that her death certificate gives her age as **90**. He says she was buried in a cemetery in **Colón, Cuba**. Since she is said to have arrived in **1863**, that would mean she lived on the island for about **72 years**, which supports the idea that she arrived as a teenager.

The speaker quotes or paraphrases **Willie Ramos** as arguing that Latuán's ritual knowledge may initially have been limited in comparison with the older priests of the era, and that she may have been initiated in Havana rather than arriving with a fully developed priestly role already established. The speaker then pushes back on that point. He argues that a thirteen-year-old from Yoruba land in the nineteenth century would not necessarily have been a blank canvas. In his view, a child from that world could have already seen ceremonies, spoken fluent Yoruba, and absorbed a great deal of ritual culture before ever arriving in Cuba.

He makes a similar argument about language. If someone like Latuán arrived from Yoruba land as a teenager, he says, she would likely have spoken **fluent Yoruba**, not broken Cuban Lucumí. So when scholars say she may have had to “learn Lucumí,” the speaker thinks that may be better understood as learning the **Cuban ritual dialect and Cubanized vocabulary**, not learning the religion from zero.

On family background, he says the household that took Latuán in was associated with the surname **Albear**, which may explain the surname by which she is remembered in some sources. He also says there are conflicting stories about her husband and naming history. One version says she married a man named **Miguel [unclear surname]**; another version connected to **David H. Brown** says her husband was **Evaristo Albear**. The speaker is explicit that the stories conflict and that he does not want to pretend certainty where the sources disagree.

He also says Latuán had children, grandchildren, and descendants. According to three grandchildren interviewed in the source he references, she remained under a limited form of emancipation or constrained freedom for about **ten years** before receiving full freedom.

One personal detail the speaker clearly loves is that Latuán was described as an **avid reader**. He says she started her day with the newspaper and was proud of being literate. He quotes a family memory that amounts to: *I may be a Black Lucumí woman, but I know the rules of literacy—I can read and write.* For him, that detail matters because literacy, education, and prestige set her apart even among already respected elders.

As for her contribution to Ocha, the speaker puts it this way: **Efunché laid the foundation, and Latuán built the house**. He says Latuán was the ritual woman behind most or all of Efunché's ordinations, and that after Efunché's death she enforced the Orthodox Havana form of Ocha for another thirty years or so. In his presentation, no initiation in Havana happened without Latuán's knowledge or approval, and she stands as proof that a woman could function in the highest ritual roles.

He also says that **Latuán and Efunché are the reason Havana-lineage people still have santo made the way they do today**. Because of that, he treats them as direct ancestors of the living ritual system.

Toward the end, he gets more reflective. He rejects the idea that Latuán was simply a blank slate molded by Efunché from nothing. His view is that Latuán probably arrived with serious knowledge from Yoruba land, and that what happened in Cuba was not the creation of a priestess from scratch, but a process of **translation, adaptation, and ritual consolidation**. In that imagined conversation, Efunché is not saying, “You know nothing and I will teach you everything,” but rather, “This is Cuba now, and we have different plants, different resources, and a creole religious environment, so we have to adapt.”

He closes by saying that English-language material on these historical figures barely exists, and even in Spanish there is not enough detailed discussion. He stresses that he puts a lot of effort into these videos because he wants to present something accurate and meaningful.

transcripts.title: Efunché Warikondó
transcripts.topic: Historical figure associated with Havana Ocha
transcripts.cleaned_transcript:
This is another history video. I got a great response to the first one, so now I'm doing one on **Efunché**.

Before jumping into her, I want to add something I forgot to mention in the last video. According to **Willie Ramos**, there is documentation showing that **Ma Monserrate** had moved by at least **1873** to **Matanzas**, because a permit was requested for a public drumming there. The date given in the transcript is **December 6, 1873**, which the speaker connects with **Changó's day / St. Barbara's day**.

The speaker says there are **zero photos** of **Efunché** or **Latuán**, so for a lot of these women we are dealing with history more than imagery.

He explains that when older Cuban usage places **Ña** or a similar title before a person's name, it can indicate an elder African-born person rather than a Cuban creole. The woman he is discussing here—**Efunché**—is presented as **Yoruba-born**, not Cuban-born.

He places her birth around **1804** and her death around **1903**, while acknowledging that other dates circulate and documentation is scarce. His working position is that **1903** is the most plausible date unless stronger evidence appears.

In his words, **Efunché is the single most influential pillar and founder of Havana Ocha as we know it today**. He frames it like this: what **Ma Monserrate** is to **Matanzas**, **Efunché** is to **Havana**. He repeatedly stresses that he is talking specifically about **Havana Ocha**, because Matanzas and Havana both matter but do not collapse into each other.

On her personal life, he says almost nothing concrete is known. We do not know what she looked like, and we know little about her day-to-day personality. What he does feel comfortable saying is that she was not a Cuban creole, but a Yoruba native, and likely from **Oyo**, because the ritual structure of Havana Ocha is so strongly Oyo-centered.

He says **Efunché may have crowned Latuán in Cuba**, though that remains speculative. If true, that would make Latuán not only her right hand but also her ritual descendant. Even without certainty on that point, he says the bond between them was extraordinarily close.

The question of Efunché's **crown orisha** is one of the places where the transcript openly shows historical disagreement. The speaker says the most common identification is **Ochosi**, but he has also seen lineages or sources connect her to **Obatalá** or even **Yewá**. His personal opinion is that **Obatalá** seems more plausible than Ochosi or Yewá, because Ochosi was comparatively rare in Cuba and Yewá even rarer, especially in Havana. Still, he does not pretend the matter is settled.

He links Efunché to the **rama de los Millonarios** and to various sub-ramas associated with **San José Ochenta / San José 80**, which he treats as a major ritual center in Havana. In the transcript, San José 80 is described as more than just a cabildo name: it was a physical house, a large colonial-style home where members lived, held ceremonies, and carried out full initiations.

He then traces a web of descendants and related figures, including **Andrea Trujillo**, who would later initiate **Susana Cantero**, showing how these lineages radiated outward while still pointing back to core female founders.

One of his more evocative reflections is linguistic. He imagines that if you had walked into that house in the late nineteenth century, you might have heard **Spanish in the street** and **Yoruba inside the cabildo**, because so many of these women were African-born. He acknowledges that this is an inference, not a documented quotation, but he presents it as a historically reasonable image.

The middle of the transcript turns into a larger argument about **lineage variation**. He says that many priests today justify all kinds of differences by saying, “In my house we do it this way.” He is not denying that small variations exist. What he challenges is the idea that Havana Ocha has endlessly divergent branches with totally separate standards. His point is that if **Efunché** stood over the ritual world of Havana, and if **Latuán** was central in the actual oriaté work, then the differences among Havana ramas should be understood as variations within a common structure, not excuses for anything and everything.

He gives an example from the years of religious persecution: because it could be dangerous to bring an initiate to the river, some houses reportedly had the future initiate remain at home in a tub while designated ritual people went to the river, performed what they could there, and brought the water back. The speaker says that kind of adaptation makes sense under pressure. What bothers him is when temporary adaptations later get frozen and defended as eternal lineage law.

Then he turns to **Efunché's contributions**.

First, he says she **laid the basic ground rules of initiation** in Havana Ocha. He links her to the system in which the initiate must receive a core set of principal orishas. In his phrasing, the initiation is not valid unless those major presences are there as witnesses. He also associates her with the symbolic importance of the major ritual colors used in the room.

Second, he says she established the original expectation that the **iyawó** would remain on the throne for **16 days**, with some people saying **21** at the maximum, and that the later reduction to **7 days** was a practical change.

Third, he credits her with **organizing the full order of ceremony**: what is done first, what is done later, how the initiate is taken to the river, how sacrifices and consecrations are structured, what songs and chants belong where, and how the whole thing coheres as **Yoko Ocha** rather than as a scattered collection of disconnected rites.

Fourth, he raises the question of the **composite odú**—whether the combined sign in shell divination was always part of the system or whether it emerged later. Here he is careful. He says some people attribute that development to **Efunché**, others to **Latuán**, and others to **Obadimeyi** or later innovation. He does not treat the matter as settled.

Finally, he gives Efunché perhaps her biggest role of all: **unifier**. In his telling, she decided that priests from different ritual branches could still work together in the same initiation. That means a godparent from one line, an oyugbona from another, and a ritual director from yet another could all collaborate without contradiction. He treats that as a conscious act of survival and brilliance: if each African-derived town or branch had stayed isolated, the religion might have fractured and died. Instead, under a common Havana umbrella, they built something durable together.

He ends on a poetic note. Even if there is no surviving photograph, and even if her grave is obscure or lost, he says **Efunché's presence is still felt every time a new iyawó is born in Havana style**. That, to him, is her living monument.

transcripts.title: Ma Monserrate González, Obá Teró (Apóto)
transcripts.topic: Historical figure associated with Havana and Matanzas Ocha
transcripts.cleaned_transcript:
Forgive the lighting—sometimes it goes in, sometimes it goes out. I wanted to do something different and talk about historical figures, because I'm very big on studying the pillars and pioneers of what we call Ocha.

So let's start with one of the main pillars: **Ma Monserrate González**, known ritually as **Obá Teró**, and associated in some sources with the name **Apóto**. The transcript itself notes that this naming can get confusing, because more than one elder may be associated with similar names in oral accounts.

The speaker places her birth around **1805** and her death somewhere between **1903 and 1907**, saying only that she was at least about **100 years old** when she died.

He identifies her as a major ancestor connected to **Fermina Gómez**, and also links her to other major figures such as **José “Pata de Palo” Urquiola**, **Josefa “Pepa” Herrera**, and **Obá Alfredo Calvo** through ritual and family memory. He makes clear that many of the names he is dropping here deserve entire videos of their own.

He says Ma Monserrate was from **Egbado**, a Yoruba region, and that she was taken to Cuba as an enslaved woman, specifically to **Regla** in the Havana area. He describes Regla as a major Black port community and an important zone for Afro-Cuban religious life.

In his framing, Ma Monserrate is one of the pillars of Ocha because she helped establish the foundation of what later became formalized Ocha in Cuba. Why? Because the **first documented full Ocha initiation in Cuba**, in his account, took place in **1864**, and Ma Monserrate was involved in that world. He specifically links that early initiation to **Josefa “Pepa” Herrera (Eshubí)**, daughter of **Adeshina**.

Then he turns to the rupture.

According to the speaker, there were major differences of ritual opinion between **Ma Monserrate** on one side and **Efunché and Latuán** on the other. Ma Monserrate represented an **Egbado-style** current of Ocha, while Havana increasingly became more **Oyo- and Changó-centered**. He says Efunché and Latuán wanted Ma Monserrate to conform her style of initiation to theirs, but she refused. With the support of **Adeshina**, she then moved from Havana to **Matanzas**.

He dates her Matanzas move to no later than **1873**, meaning that between **1864 and 1873** she would have had about nine years of work in Havana before Matanzas became her main base.

The transcript also preserves stories of conflict. Some people, he says, told stories of ritual warfare or witchcraft between Ma Monserrate and the Havana camp of Efunché and Latuán. But then he introduces a counterpoint: **Alfredo Calvo**, speaking as a descendant, said on camera that his great-grandmother remained on good terms with them and that they even attended one another's ceremonies. The speaker does not try to resolve the contradiction. He simply says the sources disagree.

As for her contributions, he starts with the big one: **Ma Monserrate helped lay the groundwork for Ocha in Cuba**. Even if later Havana standardization is associated more with Efunché, the fact remains, in his telling, that an early full kariocha happened in the world Ma Monserrate was helping shape.

He also argues that **Havana and Matanzas influenced each other**. Even after the split, the two styles did not remain sealed off from one another. Ritual ideas, implements, deity knowledge, and ceremonial structures moved back and forth.

One of the most important claims in the transcript is that Ma Monserrate exchanged knowledge with the **Arará**. The speaker says there was a transmission of shell-divination knowledge, ceremony secrets, and deity traditions between Lucumí and Arará currents. In his view, that exchange helps explain how certain beings and cultic complexes—especially those associated with **Arará/Fon** traditions—became available in Lucumí practice in Cuba.

He credits Ma Monserrate with helping carry forward the knowledge of important orishas and ritual complexes such as **Olokún**, **Oduduwá**, **Yewá**, **Babalú Ayé / Asojano**, and related currents that later became significant in both Matanzas and Havana. He stresses that some of these traditions became especially identified with **Matanzas**, but that Havana later also received elements that may not have been available without people like Ma Monserrate.

On her personal life, the speaker says she had been enslaved on an unknown plantation and reportedly spoke very little about that time in her life. That silence itself fascinates him.

He ends the transcript with a dramatic story drawn from **Frank Baba Eyiogbe's** book **Babalawo: The Secrets of Afro-Cuban Ifa**. In that story, a powerful priest named **Ño José / [unclear in source transcript]** had some conflict involving **Fermina Gómez**, and a prolonged battle of ritual aggression followed. One night, while Ma Monserrate slept, her **Changó** supposedly mounted her, rushed to the door, and interrupted an attack involving ritual powder or witchcraft placed there by her enemy. Later, during the same struggle, Changó again mounted her, took up a thunderstone, went to the enemy's doorway, raised it to the sky, and invoked the heavens until a massive storm broke over Matanzas. The next day, the rival died under mysterious circumstances.

The speaker is careful, even while telling the story, to say that he does not know what is literal fact, what is embellishment, and what is pious storytelling. But he includes it because stories like that reveal how later generations remembered the force, charisma, and sacred reputation of Ma Monserrate.

He closes by saying something he finds ironic: although **Efunché** and **Latuán** may have won the fight for Havana, the surviving **photographs** that people most often circulate are of **Ma Monserrate**, **Adeshina**, and **Fermina Gómez**, not of Efunché or Latuán. To him, that visual survival says something powerful about memory, legacy, and who still stares back at us through history.

transcripts.title: What Is Oríkì?
transcripts.topic: Explanation of oríkì in Lucumí practice
validation_notes: The transcript clearly centers on oríkì (praise poetry), not orí alone.
Key standardized terms used here include Oríkì, Òrìṣà, òrun, ayé, aṣẹ, Obí, Elegbá, Oshosí, and modúpẹ́.
The cited book title was normalized to 'Obí Agbón: Lukumi Divination With Coconut' by Obá Miguel 'Willie' Ramos, Ilarí Obá.
Some names and liturgical phrases in the source audio remain too unclear to normalize safely and are marked [unclear].
Historical or doctrinal claims in the body remain the speaker's claims unless independently verified elsewhere.
transcripts.cleaned_transcript:
What's up, it's Elen Kor back with another video. Yes, I know the lighting is bad. Yes, I know it looks like I'm filming this on a 1990s camcorder. I'm just a guy with a phone and a computer, so hopefully you enjoy the video.

Today I want to talk about **oríkì**. In other videos I want to go over topics like Odù, Òrìṣà, and related concepts, but for now I'm focusing on oríkì.

Oríkì is a **praise poem**—words of praise or flattery used to call, honor, and incentivize the presence of a given Òrìṣà. Oríkì is recited whenever we cast **obí**. It is recited over a person's head for head rogations, during major ceremonies such as the river ceremony and a full kariosha, when dealing with sacred plants, during divination—whether through diloggún or obí—and also simply to give general praise to the Òrìṣà. Whenever I prostrate to my Òrìṣà, I try to recite oríkì. We hear words of praise to the Òrìṣà being consulted or acknowledged at different points in ritual.

There is a misunderstanding that the Òrìṣà are just hanging around 24/7 because you have your warriors behind the door or your santos somewhere in the house. The speaker argues that this is not the case. Just because someone has received warriors does not mean those powers are actively present in every moment. Just because someone is crowned Obatalá does not mean Obatalá is automatically present every second.

The speaker explains this by saying that the Òrìṣà reside in **òrun**, the invisible or heavenly realm, while the physical representations we receive on earth are the bodies or vessels through which that power may be called into **ayé**, the world. He uses **Elegbá** as an example: the consecrated object is a physical representation and vessel, but that does not mean the active presence of the deity is always there in a literal, immediate sense.

To make that presence active, one must call it. That is where oríkì comes in. Through praise, offerings, sound, and other ritual media—such as rum, palm oil, cigar smoke, and instruments or noise-makers—the invisible aṣẹ of the Òrìṣà is called from òrun into ayé.

The speaker notes that in Yorùbá practice in Nigeria, oríkì can be long, complex, musical, and antiphonal, with a lead and chorus. He describes it as beautiful praise poetry, sometimes going on for many minutes with stanza after stanza praising the deity. By contrast, in Cuban Lucumí practice, oríkì is often delivered more like spoken-word ritual poetry by a single officiant while others remain silent and listen.

He then makes a broader point: most people outside of their immediate elders or a knowledgeable babalawo do not know how to recite much oríkì. If they know any at all, they often know only a short version—just enough to perform a head rogation or basic devotional act. In the old days, he says, this kind of knowledge was more widespread among santeros and santeras, not only among oriatés. Over time, many practitioners have become heavily dependent on oriatés for the language, songs, history, herbs, ceremonial order, and other specialized knowledge. He also argues that many people have falling-outs with elders or are abandoned by their godparents, and that this contributes to a cycle in which poorly taught practitioners later teach others poorly.

He says there is not enough emphasis on this body of ritual language today. In his view, many people know only the shortest invocations, while the longer forms go largely unmemorized.

The speaker then gives an example involving **Obatalá**. He says that in many places one hears only a very short, common invocation, and that people stop there and move on. By contrast, the longer versions are much more extensive. He does not fully reproduce them in the cleaned transcript, but his point is that most people do not memorize the long form unless they grew up immersed in the religion every day.

He also emphasizes that learning these texts takes repetition and consistency. He says he is still learning them himself and does not pretend otherwise.

Another of his main claims is that oríkì used to be considered something all santeros and santeras should know, not something restricted only to oriatés. He says that in earlier practice, multiple praise poems were recited in major rites. For example, during the river ceremony connected with kariosha, he says that praise poems for many Òrìṣà—he gives the number as twenty-one—were recited in a specific order. He says this is something he personally has not seen in practice, and he attributes that absence to the fact that many people today do not know even a single oríkì well.

He makes a similar point about head rogation. In his view, a knowledgeable officiant may recite far more than the brief formula that most people hear. He says some officiants recite many invocations over a person's head, including invocations tied not only to Òrìṣà but also to **Odù**. He specifically mentions an elder named **David [surname unclear]** as someone he knows of who recites praise formulas for the sixteen singular Odù over a person's head during rogation.

The speaker argues that Odù, like Òrìṣà, is living spiritual force, and that praise language is also a way of calling that force into presence so it can guide and bless the person.

He then returns to head rogation and says that rogation is not merely about physically cooling or feeding the head. In his view, it is also about appealing to the aṣẹ of **Obatalá**, the shaper or owner of the head, and calling that energy into presence through speech, song, and praise. He says there are songs to the head, songs to Obatalá, and even songs to the moon that could be included in a much deeper version of the rite, though most people today learn only the basics.

From there he broadens the lesson into a devotional recommendation: anyone who has received Òrìṣà—whether crowned or not, whether they have only the warriors or a single deity—would benefit from learning the proper oríkì for the powers they serve. He encourages people to ask their godparent for the praise poems appropriate to their own Òrìṣà.

Using **Elegbá** as an example, he says many people faithfully give palm oil, rum, and smoke every Monday but never recite a single praise poem to actually call Elegbá from òrun to hear their prayers and carry them upward.

He then addresses the common opening prayer that many people say with water at the beginning of ritual. In his explanation, that opening is an act of respect and cooling—a way of laying out the red carpet, so to speak—but not the same thing as fully inviting the presence of the deity to arrive and participate.

He uses **obí** divination to make this concrete. Before jumping into questions, he says, one first asks whether Elegbá is present and ready to be consulted. If the answer is negative, one does not simply proceed as if nothing happened. Instead, he says, one continues to praise, offer, and call until there is an affirmative response.

A major point in the latter part of the talk is that oríkì is not only flattering language. It is also **instructional**. By studying praise poetry, one learns the nature, habits, temperament, and attributes of the Òrìṣà.

He gives **Oba** as an example. He paraphrases lines he learned for Oba as something like: **the patient one who eats she-goat early in the morning; she who walks with witches in the middle of the night.** His point is that this is not decorative language alone. From those lines, he says, one learns that Oba is patient, associated with she-goat in his lineage, and deeply linked with the world of witches and nocturnal power. In other words, the praise poem teaches theology, character, and ritual association all at once.

He contrasts that with the way some people casually describe other Òrìṣà as witches while not being able to point to similar explicit references in the praise poetry they themselves have learned. For him, that makes Oba's oríkì especially revealing.

Toward the end, he explains where he has been learning some of these materials. He cites a book by **Obá Miguel “Willie” Ramos** that he identifies as **Obí Agbón: Lukumi Divination With Coconut**. He says the book contains a number of oríkì in the back, though not necessarily in the ceremonial order in which they would be recited during a full ritual sequence.

He also says he does not want to make videos that simply give away the contents of another author's work for free. He wants people to support the author and buy the book if they want the material in full.

He closes by encouraging viewers to talk with their godparents, study seriously, and deepen their relationship with the Òrìṣà through proper praise and invocation. He ends with **modúpẹ́**, which he glosses as "I am grateful."

validation_notes: Willie Ramos = Obá Miguel 'Willie' Ramos; book title normalized to 'Orí Eledá Mí Ó… If My Head Does Not Sell Me.'
David H. Brown title normalized to 'Santería Enthroned.'

Timotea 'Latuán' Albear, Efunché/Efunshé Warikondó, Ma Monserrate González (Obá Teró / Apóto), Fermina Gómez, José 'Pata de Palo' Urquiola, Obadimeyi / Octavio Samá, Margarita Armenteros (Aina), and San José 80 were standardized from public-source spellings.
Some names and narrative details remained too unclear to normalize confidently and are marked [unclear].
